chapterTitle: The Lamb Opens the Six Seals
themeTitle: “How Long, Master, the Holy and True?”

scripture.text: I saw that the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures saying, as with a voice of thunder, “Come and see!”
scripture.understanding: Καὶ εἶδον ὅτε ἤνοιξεν τὸ ἀρνίον μίαν ἐκ τῶν ἑπτὰ σφραγίδων, “I saw that the Lamb opened one of the seven seals” — εἴδω, from the see family (and the know family); ἀρνίον, from the lamb family. Every judgement that follows is released by the Lamb: nothing happens outside His control. καὶ ἤκουσα ἑνὸς ἐκ τῶν τεσσάρων ζῴων λέγοντος ὡς φωνὴ βροντῆς· Ἔρχου, “and I heard one of the four living creatures saying, as with a voice of thunder, ‘Come and see!’” — ἔρχου, ‘Come!’ is addressed to the rider; ‘and see’ (βλέπε, from the see family) is found in later manuscripts.

scripture.text: And behold, a white horse, and he who sat on it had a bow. A crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.
scripture.understanding: καὶ εἶδον, καὶ ἰδοὺ ἵππος λευκός, “And behold, a white horse” — εἴδω, from the see family (and the know family). Zechariah saw horses of different colours sent through the earth (Zechariah 1:8; 6:2–3). καὶ ὁ καθήμενος ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν ἔχων τόξον, “and he who sat on it had a bow” — τόξον, the weapon of the feared Parthian horsemen on Rome's eastern frontier. καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ στέφανος, “A crown was given to him” — στέφανος, from the crown family: a victor's wreath. καὶ ἐξῆλθεν νικῶν καὶ ἵνα νικήσῃ, “and he came out conquering, and to conquer” — νικάω. Some see this rider as Christ or the gospel going out (19:11); but since the other three horsemen bring war, famine and death, the strongest reading is conquest and military aggression — perhaps a counterfeit of Christ, white on the outside, conquering by force.

scripture.text: When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying, “Come!”
scripture.understanding: Καὶ ὅτε ἤνοιξεν τὴν σφραγῖδα τὴν δευτέραν, “When he opened the second seal” — σφραγίς. ἤκουσα τοῦ δευτέρου ζῴου λέγοντος· Ἔρχου, “I heard the second living creature saying, ‘Come!’” — each creature in turn summons a rider. Heaven commands; the horsemen obey.

scripture.text: Another came out, a red horse. To him who sat on it was given power to take peace from the earth, and that they should kill one another. There was given to him a great sword.
scripture.understanding: καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ἄλλος ἵππος πυρρός, “Another came out, a red horse” — πυρρός, fiery red, the colour of blood. καὶ τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν ἐδόθη αὐτῷ λαβεῖν τὴν εἰρήνην ἐκ τῆς γῆς, “To him who sat on it was given power to take peace from the earth” — γῆ, from the world family. The Pax Romana, Rome's boasted peace, can be taken away in a moment. καὶ ἵνα ἀλλήλους σφάξουσιν, “and that they should kill one another” — σφάζω, the word used of the slain Lamb (5:6): civil war, mutual slaughter. καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ μάχαιρα μεγάλη, “There was given to him a great sword” — μάχαιρα, from the sword family: the short sword of soldiers and executions, as distinct from the ῥομφαία of Christ's mouth (1:16).

scripture.text: When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying, “Come and see!” And behold, a black horse, and he who sat on it had a balance in his hand.
scripture.understanding: Καὶ ὅτε ἤνοιξεν τὴν σφραγῖδα τὴν τρίτην, “When he opened the third seal” — σφραγίς. καὶ εἶδον, καὶ ἰδοὺ ἵππος μέλας, “And behold, a black horse” — εἴδω, from the see family (and the know family). μέλας, black: the colour of mourning and famine. καὶ ὁ καθήμενος ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν ἔχων ζυγὸν ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὐτοῦ, “and he who sat on it had a balance in his hand” — ζυγός, a pair of scales: food is being weighed out and rationed.

scripture.text: I heard a voice in the middle of the four living creatures saying, “A choenix of wheat for a denarius, and three choenix of barley for a denarius! Don’t damage the oil and the wine!”
scripture.understanding: Χοῖνιξ σίτου δηναρίου, “A choenix of wheat for a denarius” — a χοῖνιξ, about a litre, was one man's daily ration of grain; a denarius was a full day's wage. A day's work buys only enough bread for one person: famine prices. καὶ τρεῖς χοίνικες κριθῆς δηναρίου, “and three choenix of barley for a denarius!” — barley was the poor man's grain, enough for a small family. καὶ τὸ ἔλαιον καὶ τὸν οἶνον μὴ ἀδικήσῃς, “Don’t damage the oil and the wine!” — ἀδικέω, to harm. Olive trees and vines have deep roots and survive drought; or perhaps the luxuries of the rich are untouched while the poor go hungry. The judgement is limited.

scripture.text: When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the fourth living creature saying, “Come and see!”
scripture.understanding: Καὶ ὅτε ἤνοιξεν τὴν σφραγῖδα τὴν τετάρτην, “When he opened the fourth seal” — σφραγίς. ἤκουσα φωνὴν τοῦ τετάρτου ζῴου λέγοντος· Ἔρχου, “I heard the fourth living creature saying, ‘Come and see!’” — ἔρχου; ‘and see’ (βλέπε, from the see family) appears in later manuscripts.

scripture.text: And behold, a pale horse, and he who sat on it, his name was Death. Hades followed with him. Authority over one fourth of the earth, to kill with the sword, with famine, with death, and by the wild animals of the earth was given to him.
scripture.understanding: καὶ εἶδον, καὶ ἰδοὺ ἵππος χλωρός, “And behold, a pale horse” — εἴδω, from the see family (and the know family). χλωρός, the yellowish-green of a corpse. καὶ ὁ καθήμενος ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ, ὄνομα αὐτῷ ὁ Θάνατος, καὶ ὁ ᾅδης ἠκολούθει μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ, “and he who sat on it, his name was Death. Hades followed with him” — death takes the body, Hades the soul. But Christ holds their keys (1:18). καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτοῖς ἐξουσία ἐπὶ τὸ τέταρτον τῆς γῆς, “Authority over one fourth of the earth” — ἐξουσία, from the power family: delegated authority — given, and limited; γῆ, from the world family. ἀποκτεῖναι ἐν ῥομφαίᾳ καὶ ἐν λιμῷ καὶ ἐν θανάτῳ καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν θηρίων τῆς γῆς, “to kill with the sword, with famine, with death, and by the wild animals of the earth” — ῥομφαία, from the sword family; θάνατος here means plague. Ezekiel's ‘four severe judgements’: sword, famine, wild beasts and plague.

scripture.text: When he opened the fifth seal, I saw underneath the altar the souls of those who had been killed for the Word of God, and for the testimony of the Lamb which they had.
scripture.understanding: Καὶ ὅτε ἤνοιξεν τὴν πέμπτην σφραγῖδα, εἶδον ὑποκάτω τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου, “When he opened the fifth seal, I saw underneath the altar” — εἴδω, from the see family (and the know family); θυσιαστήριον, the altar: in the temple the blood of sacrifices was poured out at the base of the altar. τὰς ψυχὰς τῶν ἐσφαγμένων διὰ τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ, “the souls of those who had been killed for the Word of God” — ψυχή, from the life family: the life, the person; σφάζω, the word used of the Lamb (5:6): they died as He died; λόγος, from the word family. καὶ διὰ τὴν μαρτυρίαν ἣν εἶχον, “and for the testimony of the Lamb which they had” — μαρτυρία, from the witness family.

scripture.text: They cried with a loud voice, saying, “How long, Master, the holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?”
scripture.understanding: καὶ ἔκραξαν φωνῇ μεγάλῃ λέγοντες, “They cried with a loud voice, saying” — κράζω, to cry out. Ἕως πότε, ὁ δεσπότης ὁ ἅγιος καὶ ἀληθινός, “How long, Master, the holy and true” — the cry of the psalms. δεσπότης, absolute master, the owner of slaves; ἅγιος and ἀληθινός, the titles of Christ in 3:7. οὐ κρίνεις καὶ ἐκδικεῖς τὸ αἷμα ἡμῶν, “until you judge and avenge our blood” — κρίνω, from the judge family: to try and decide; ἐκδικέω, to vindicate, to do justice. Not personal revenge, but a plea for God to put things right publicly. ἐκ τῶν κατοικούντων ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, “on those who dwell on the earth” — γῆ, from the world family: Revelation's phrase for those who oppose God. ἅγιος is from the holy family — holy, set apart for God; as a noun, the saints — God’s holy people.

scripture.text: A long white robe was given to each of them. They were told that they should rest yet for a while, until their fellow servants and their brothers, who would also be killed even as they were, should complete their course.
scripture.understanding: καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτοῖς ἑκάστῳ στολὴ λευκή, “A long white robe was given to each of them” — στολή, the long robe of honour: the white garments promised to the overcomers (3:5). They are already vindicated in heaven. καὶ ἐρρέθη αὐτοῖς ἵνα ἀναπαύσονται ἔτι χρόνον μικρόν, “They were told that they should rest yet for a while” — ἀναπαύω, from the rest family; χρόνος, from the time family: a short span of time. ἕως πληρωθῶσιν καὶ οἱ σύνδουλοι αὐτῶν, “until their fellow servants and their brothers... should complete their course” — πληρόω, from the perfect family: to be made full, completed; σύνδουλος, a fellow slave. God has an appointed number; His patience is not neglect.

scripture.text: I saw when he opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake. The sun became black as sackcloth made of hair, and the whole moon became as blood.
scripture.understanding: Καὶ εἶδον ὅτε ἤνοιξεν τὴν σφραγῖδα τὴν ἕκτην, “I saw when he opened the sixth seal” — εἴδω, from the see family (and the know family). καὶ σεισμὸς μέγας ἐγένετο, “and there was a great earthquake” — σεισμός: the cities of Asia knew earthquakes well (Sardis and Philadelphia were devastated in AD 17). καὶ ὁ ἥλιος ἐγένετο μέλας ὡς σάκκος τρίχινος, “The sun became black as sackcloth made of hair” — σάκκος, the rough black cloth of mourning. καὶ ἡ σελήνη ὅλη ἐγένετο ὡς αἷμα, “and the whole moon became as blood” — the prophets' language for the day of the Lord, which Peter quoted at Pentecost (Acts 2:20).

scripture.text: The stars of the sky fell to the earth, like a fig tree dropping its unripe figs when it is shaken by a great wind.
scripture.understanding: καὶ οἱ ἀστέρες τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἔπεσαν εἰς τὴν γῆν, “The stars of the sky fell to the earth” — γῆ, from the world family. ὡς συκῆ βάλλει τοὺς ὀλύνθους αὐτῆς ὑπὸ ἀνέμου μεγάλου σειομένη, “like a fig tree dropping its unripe figs when it is shaken by a great wind” — ὄλυνθος, the late, unripe winter figs. Isaiah used the same picture of the heavens' host falling like fruit from a fig tree. The created order seems to come apart.

scripture.text: The sky was removed like a scroll when it is rolled up. Every mountain and island were moved out of their places.
scripture.understanding: καὶ ὁ οὐρανὸς ἀπεχωρίσθη ὡς βιβλίον ἑλισσόμενον, “The sky was removed like a scroll when it is rolled up” — βιβλίον, from the book family: the same word as the Lamb's scroll; ἑλίσσω, to roll up. The sky that seemed eternal is rolled away like a finished document (Isaiah 34:4). καὶ πᾶν ὄρος καὶ νῆσος ἐκ τῶν τόπων αὐτῶν ἐκινήθησαν, “Every mountain and island were moved out of their places” — κινέω, the word used of Ephesus' lampstand (2:5). Nothing in creation is permanent except God.

scripture.text: The kings of the earth, the princes, the commanding officers, the rich, the strong, and every slave and free person, hid themselves in the caves and in the rocks of the mountains.
scripture.understanding: καὶ οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς καὶ οἱ μεγιστᾶνες καὶ οἱ χιλίαρχοι καὶ οἱ πλούσιοι καὶ οἱ ἰσχυροί, “The kings of the earth, the princes, the commanding officers, the rich, the strong” — γῆ, from the world family; ἰσχυρός, from the power family: the mighty in physical force. καὶ πᾶς δοῦλος καὶ ἐλεύθερος, “and every slave and free person” — δοῦλος, from the servant family. Seven classes, from emperor to slave: all humanity without God, from top to bottom. ἔκρυψαν ἑαυτοὺς εἰς τὰ σπήλαια καὶ εἰς τὰς πέτρας τῶν ὀρέων, “hid themselves in the caves and in the rocks of the mountains” — as Isaiah foresaw people hiding in the rocks ‘from the terror of the LORD’.

scripture.text: They told the mountains and the rocks, “Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him who sits on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb,
scripture.understanding: καὶ λέγουσιν τοῖς ὄρεσιν καὶ ταῖς πέτραις· Πέσετε ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς, “They told the mountains and the rocks, ‘Fall on us’” — Hosea's words, which Jesus quoted on the way to the cross (Luke 23:30). καὶ κρύψατε ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ καθημένου ἐπὶ τοῦ θρόνου, “and hide us from the face of him who sits on the throne” — the face His people long to see (22:4) is the face His enemies cannot bear. καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς τοῦ ἀρνίου, “and from the wrath of the Lamb” — ὀργή, from the wrath family: settled, holy anger, as distinct from θυμός, anger as a passionate outburst; ἀρνίον, from the lamb family. The most startling phrase in the book: the gentlest of creatures, angry. Rejected love becomes judgement.

scripture.text: for the great day of his wrath has come; and who is able to stand?”
scripture.understanding: ὅτι ἦλθεν ἡ ἡμέρα ἡ μεγάλη τῆς ὀργῆς αὐτῶν, “for the great day of his wrath has come” — ἡμέρα, from the time family: ‘the day of the LORD’ of the prophets; ὀργή, from the wrath family. Many manuscripts read ‘their wrath’ — of God and the Lamb together. καὶ τίς δύναται σταθῆναι; “and who is able to stand?” — δύναμαι, from the power family: who has the ability? The question is left hanging — and chapter 7 answers it.

visualMeditations.title: Four Horsemen
visualMeditations.image: Picture four horses galloping out from the throne one after another: a white horse whose rider draws a bow, a red horse whose rider swings a great sword, a black horse whose rider holds up a pair of scales, and a sickly pale horse ridden by Death, with the grave following behind.
visualMeditations.meaning: “I saw that the Lamb opened one of the seven seals” (v. 1). Conquest, war, famine and death are the familiar sorrows of a fallen world. Revelation does not deny them, but it shows that even they are released and limited by the Lamb — ‘authority over one fourth of the earth’, and no more (v. 8).

visualMeditations.title: Souls Under the Altar
visualMeditations.image: Picture the great altar of heaven, and at its base, where the blood of sacrifices was poured, the souls of martyrs crying out. Then see an angel moving among them, placing a long white robe on each one, and speaking quietly: ‘Rest a little longer.’
visualMeditations.meaning: “How long, Master, the holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” (v. 10). “A long white robe was given to each of them. They were told that they should rest yet for a while” (v. 11). God hears the cry for justice. His delay is not indifference; it is patience with a plan.

visualMeditations.title: The Sky Rolled Up
visualMeditations.image: Picture the ground heaving, the sun going black, the moon turning blood-red, stars falling like figs shaken from a tree in a gale — and the sky itself rolled up like a scroll, leaving nothing above but God.
visualMeditations.meaning: “The sky was removed like a scroll when it is rolled up. Every mountain and island were moved out of their places” (v. 14). Everything people trust as solid and permanent can be moved. Only God and those who are His stand firm.

visualMeditations.title: Hiding from the Lamb
visualMeditations.image: Picture emperors, generals, billionaires, soldiers and slaves all crowding into the same caves, begging the mountains to fall on them. Not because of an army, but because they have seen a face on a throne and a Lamb whose patience has ended.
visualMeditations.meaning: “Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him who sits on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of his wrath has come; and who is able to stand?” (vv. 16–17). Only those sheltered by the Lamb's blood can stand before the Lamb's wrath.

structure.label: The Four Horsemen (v. 1-8)
structure.body: The Lamb opens the first four seals; at each a living creature calls out, and a rider goes forth: on a white horse with a bow and a crown, conquering; on a red horse with a great sword, taking peace from the earth; on a black horse with scales, bringing famine prices; on a pale horse, Death, with Hades following, given authority over a quarter of the earth.

structure.label: The Cry of the Martyrs (v. 9-11)
structure.body: At the fifth seal John sees under the altar the souls of those slain for God's word and their testimony; they cry out for God to judge and avenge their blood; each is given a white robe and told to rest a little longer until the number of their fellow servants is complete.

structure.label: The Great Day of Wrath (v. 12-17)
structure.body: At the sixth seal there is a great earthquake; the sun goes black, the moon turns to blood, the stars fall, the sky is rolled up and mountains and islands move; everyone from kings to slaves hides in the caves and begs the mountains to hide them from the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of wrath has come.

sections.heading: The Lamb Opens the Seals
paragraphs: The scroll is now in the Lamb's hand, and He begins to open it: “I saw that the Lamb opened one of the seven seals” (v. 1). This is the first of three series of seven judgements in Revelation — seals (chs. 6–8), trumpets (chs. 8–11) and bowls (ch. 16). Each series grows more intense: the seals affect a quarter of the earth (6:8), the trumpets a third (8:7–12), the bowls the whole (16:1–21). Many see the three series as overlapping views of the same period, each ending at the end of history; others see them as following one another in sequence.

Whatever the order, the main point is clear. These terrible things do not happen because God has lost control. The Lamb opens each seal; a living creature from the throne calls each rider; the power of each is ‘given’ (vv. 2, 4, 8). Evil is real, but it runs on a leash held by the Lamb.

Jesus spoke of the same things: “You will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you aren’t troubled, for all this must happen, but the end is not yet” (Matthew 24:6), and “nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there will be famines, plagues, and earthquakes in various places. But all these things are the beginning of birth pains” (Matthew 24:7–8). The four horsemen picture the sorrows that run through all history between Christ's first and second comings.

sections.heading: The Four Horsemen
paragraphs: The first rider, on a white horse, carries a bow and wears a crown, and “he came out conquering, and to conquer” (v. 2). Because Christ later rides a white horse (19:11), some see here the victorious spread of the gospel. But this rider belongs with the three that follow, which all bring disaster; and his weapon is a bow, not the sword of Christ's mouth. The strongest reading is that he represents conquest and the lust for power — perhaps a counterfeit of Christ, looking righteous but conquering by force.

The second rider takes peace from the earth so that people kill one another (v. 4). The third brings famine: “A choenix of wheat for a denarius” (v. 6) — a whole day's wage for one person's daily bread. Yet the oil and wine are spared: the judgement is real but limited. The fourth rider is Death himself, followed by Hades, and they are given authority “over one fourth of the earth, to kill with the sword, with famine, with death, and by the wild animals of the earth” (v. 8).

Conquest, war, famine and death: this is what human sin and rebellion produce in a fallen world. God does not need to invent new punishments; He often lets sin run its course. But He sets limits — one quarter, no more — and these sorrows are meant to warn and to call people to repentance (9:20–21).

sections.heading: How Long?
paragraphs: The fifth seal moves from earth to heaven. John sees “underneath the altar the souls of those who had been killed for the Word of God, and for the testimony of the Lamb which they had” (v. 9). Their blood was poured out like a sacrifice; they were ‘slain’ with the same word used of the Lamb. Their cry is the cry of the oppressed in every age: “How long, Master, the holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” (v. 10).

This is not a cry for personal revenge. It is a plea that God would show Himself to be what He is — holy and true — by putting things right in public. Jesus promised, “Won’t God avenge his chosen ones, who are crying out to him day and night, and yet he exercises patience with them? I tell you that he will avenge them quickly” (Luke 18:7–8). Paul told believers, “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath” (Romans 12:19).

God's answer comes in two parts: a white robe for each, and a word of patience: “they should rest yet for a while, until their fellow servants and their brothers, who would also be killed even as they were, should complete their course” (v. 11). They are already vindicated in heaven; their full public vindication waits for God's appointed time. The rest of the book is, in a sense, the answer to their prayer.

sections.heading: The Great Day of Wrath
paragraphs: The sixth seal brings the collapse of the universe: earthquake, a black sun, a blood-red moon, falling stars, the sky rolled up like a scroll, mountains and islands moved (vv. 12–14). These are the prophets' pictures of the day of the Lord, used by Jesus too: “There will be signs in the sun, moon, and stars; and on the earth anxiety of nations” (Luke 21:25). Whether taken literally or as pictures of the overthrow of the powers of this world, they announce that the end has come.

Every class of person, from kings to slaves, tries to hide: “Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him who sits on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb” (v. 16). The phrase ‘the wrath of the Lamb’ holds together what we often separate. The Lamb who died for sinners is also the Judge of those who refuse Him. His wrath is ὀργή — not a loss of temper, but the settled, holy opposition of love to everything that destroys.

The chapter ends with a question: “for the great day of his wrath has come; and who is able to stand?” (v. 17). It is left hanging — and the next chapter answers it. Those who can stand are those sealed by God and washed in the blood of the Lamb (7:3, 14).

ntConnection.heading: The Beginning of Birth Pains
paragraphs: The seals follow the order of Jesus' teaching on the Mount of Olives: false messiahs, wars, famines, plagues, earthquakes, persecution and martyrdom, and finally cosmic signs and the coming of the Son of Man. “But all these things are the beginning of birth pains” (Matthew 24:8). Pain, yes — but the pain of birth, leading to new creation.

On His way to the cross, Jesus told the weeping women of Jerusalem that days were coming when people would say, “Then they will begin to tell the mountains, ‘Fall on us!’ and tell the hills, ‘Cover us.’” (Luke 23:30). The sixth seal shows that cry on a universal scale.

Paul promised suffering believers that God would act: “Since it is a righteous thing with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and to give relief to you who are afflicted with us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire” (2 Thessalonians 1:6–7). The souls under the altar receive the first part of that relief — rest and white robes — while they wait for the rest.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “properly, desire (as a reaching forth or excitement of the mind), i.e. (by analogy), violent passion (ire, or (justifiable) abhorrence); by implication punishment.” ὀργή, from the wrath family, is settled, purposeful anger — God's just and steady opposition to evil, which ends in punishment. Its sibling θυμός is anger as a boiling passion. ‘The wrath of the Lamb’ (v. 16) is not a contradiction: the same love that died for sinners must oppose everything that destroys those it loves. Those who refuse the Lamb's mercy meet the Lamb's judgement.

Strong's: “a knife, i.e. dirk; figuratively, war, judicial punishment.” μάχαιρα, from the sword family, is the soldier's short sword — and the symbol of the state's power to punish (Romans 13:4). The red horse's rider receives ‘a great μάχαιρα’ to take peace from the earth. The beast's wound is from a μάχαιρα (13:14). But Christ's weapon is always the ῥομφαία, the long sword that comes from His mouth (1:16; 19:15): He conquers not by violence but by His word.

Strong's: “a place of sacrifice, i.e. an altar (special or genitive case, literal or figurative).” θυσιαστήριον, from θυσία (sacrifice), was where offerings were made and where blood was poured out at the base. The martyrs are ‘under the altar’: their deaths are seen as sacrifices offered to God. In chapter 8 the incense of the saints' prayers rises from the golden altar, and fire from it is thrown on the earth (8:3–5). In 16:7 the altar itself speaks: ‘true and righteous are your judgments’. Their prayers are being answered.

Strong's: “an absolute ruler ("despot").” δεσπότης is the master of a household with full rights over his slaves. The martyrs address God this way: He has absolute authority over all, including their persecutors. Jude and 2 Peter use the same word for Christ, ‘the Master who bought them’ (2 Peter 2:1). To call God δεσπότης is to say: You own everything, You can act — so how long?

Strong's: “to vindicate, retaliate, punish.” ἐκδικέω, from ἐκ (out of) and δίκη (justice), means to bring justice out — to vindicate the wronged and punish the wrongdoer. The martyrs ask God to do it (6:10); in 19:2 heaven rejoices that He ‘has avenged the blood of his servants’ at Babylon's fall. Believers are told not to avenge themselves (Romans 12:19) precisely because God will; the cry of the martyrs hands justice over to Him.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: In this chapter the Holy Spirit shows you that even the darkest events of history are on a leash held by the Lamb.

items.title: The Lamb Holds the Seals
items.body: War, famine, disease and disaster are frightening. But every rider goes out only when “the Lamb opened one of the seven seals” (v. 1), and each is given limited power. The Spirit wants you to face the news of the world without panic: the One who holds the seals loves you.

items.title: Bring Your ‘How Long?’ to God
items.body: The martyrs cry, “How long, Master?” (v. 10), and God does not rebuke them. He gives them white robes and rest. The Spirit invites you to bring your own cry for justice and your own impatience honestly to God — and to receive His comfort while you wait.

items.title: Who Can Stand?
items.body: When the great day of wrath comes, the question will be, “Who is able to stand?” (v. 17). The Spirit wants you to know the answer now: no one stands by their power, wealth or position. You stand only by the blood of the Lamb. Make sure you are sheltered there.

audit.title: The Fear Check
audit.body: Which of the four horsemen — conquest, war, famine, death — do you most fear? How does knowing that the Lamb opens the seals change that fear (v. 1)?

audit.title: The Justice Check
audit.body: Is there a wrong done to you or others that you are trying to avenge yourself? Can you hand it to the holy and true Master (v. 10)?

audit.title: The Hiding Check
audit.body: Are you hiding anything from the face of God? Would you be among those running to the caves, or those running to the Lamb (vv. 16–17)?

practices.title: Pray for the Persecuted
practices.body: This week, find out about one country where Christians are being killed for their faith. Pray daily with the martyrs' words, ‘How long, Master?’, and ask God to strengthen those who suffer and to bring justice and repentance.

practices.title: Release Your Revenge
practices.body: Write down the name of someone who has wronged you. Pray over it: ‘Master, holy and true, I give this to You. You will judge rightly.’ Then pray a blessing over that person, and do one kind thing for them if you can.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, Lamb of God, You hold the scroll and You open the seals. When I hear of wars and rumours of wars, of famine and plague and death, keep me from fear, because nothing happens outside Your hand. Thank You that every power of evil is given limits by You. Holy and true Master, I join the cry of Your martyrs: how long? Look on Your suffering people across the world, and bring justice in Your time. Thank You for the white robes You give them, and for the rest they have with You. Teach me patience while I wait, and keep me faithful. Lord, when the great day of Your wrath comes and the sky is rolled up like a scroll, I do not want to hide from Your face; I want to run to it. Hide me in Your blood, Lamb of God, so that I may stand. Amen.”

storyConnections.title: Zechariah's Horses and Chariots
storyConnections.summary: In a night vision Zechariah saw “a man riding on a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in a ravine; and behind him there were red, brown, and white horses” (Zechariah 1:8). Later he saw four chariots with red, black, white and dappled horses, which were “the four winds of the sky, which go out from standing before the Lord of all the earth” (Zechariah 6:5). The horses patrolled the earth on God's behalf. Revelation's four horsemen draw on Zechariah's vision: the forces at work in the world go out from the presence of God and under His command.

storyConnections.title: Abel's Blood Cries Out
storyConnections.summary: When Cain murdered his brother Abel in the field, God said to him, ‘The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.’ The first martyr's blood called for justice, and God heard it. The souls under the altar continue that cry — and Hebrews tells us that the blood of Jesus ‘speaks better than that of Abel’ (Hebrews 12:24): it cries not only for justice but for mercy.

storyConnections.title: The Day of Pentecost
storyConnections.summary: On the day the Holy Spirit came, Peter explained what was happening by quoting the prophet Joel: “The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes” (Acts 2:20). Then he added the promise: “It will be that whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Acts 2:21). The signs of the sixth seal are the signs of that great day; but before it comes, the door of salvation is open to everyone who calls on the Lord.
